doc.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History

title: Arranging for Benny Goodman's first big band and the Let's Dance broadcasts
summary: Carter arranged for Goodman at the Billy Rose Music Hall, perhaps before Fletcher Henderson did.

story.theme_name: Writing and arranging: how musicians compose
story.community_name: Writing, arranging and composing: how the music gets made

blocks.x: You began to do some arranging outside; well, you were doing that all along, but it seems that this intensified sort of as the band began to disintegrate or as work was beginning to become more sparse. I’d like to, since we did just mention Benny Goodman, one thing you were doing in 1934, you began to arrange for his first big band.
Yeah, that’s when they were at the Billy Rose Music Hall [phonetic], before he even got the radio show. What was that show?
Let’s Dance?
You Need a Biscuit [phonetic] or something? Let’s Dance, huh?
King Biscuit or something?
Something. I don’t know. Yeah.
And then the famous Let’s Dance broadcasts.
Famous Let’s Dance broadcasts. That’s right.
Do you remember how that association as one of Goodman’s arrangers might have happened?
No, I don’t remember. These things just come . . . you know, they happen and . . .
What about your actual acquaintance with Benny Goodman? Had you already met him well before that?
Yeah, I think I met him with and through John Hammond.

When you began to arrange for the Let’s Dance broadcasts, and this is something that seems to have almost been overlooked entirely. Everyone thinks Benny Goodman, Fletcher Henderson, that’s it. But you actually arranged for the Goodman orchestra before Fletcher Henderson did, and were the first arranger for this orchestra that he took into Billy Rose and . . .
I don’t know that I was the first arranger. I’m sure someone else was doing work for him, too.
And for the Let’s Dance broadcasts, did he tell you sort of what he wanted, in terms of types of arrangements?

I don’t remember that he did, and I think the reason for that is that he was still searching. You know, wanting to listen to what anyone would do, and then he could say, “That’s it.” So that’s probably what happened with Henderson, Fletcher. When he heard Fletcher sing, he said, “Gee, that’s it. That’s what I want.”
When you arranged for this Goodman orchestra, did you ever rehearse them on your material?
I was probably there, but I don’t remember. That’s a long time ago. [laughter]
Well, this is all a long time ago.
Yeah, that’s what I’m saying, yeah.
